#+title: Ultimate GPS HAT
#+description: Adafruit Ultimate GPS HAT for the Raspberry Pi.
#+icon: Satellite

[[https://www.adafruit.com/product/2324][Adafruit Ultimate GPS HAT]] — a
GPS receiver that stacks on the Raspberry Pi's 40-pin header, with a battery
backup for warm starts.

#+ATTR_HTML: :alt Adafruit Ultimate GPS HAT
[[/adafruit-ultimate-gps-hat.jpg]]

* Specifications

Built around the MediaTek PA1616D (MT3333) module.

| Parameter         | Value            |
|-------------------+------------------|
| Satellite systems | GPS + GLONASS    |
| Channels          | 66 tracking / 99 search |
| Update rate       | up to 10 Hz      |
| Sensitivity       | −165 dBm         |
| Backup battery    | CR1220 coin cell |

* Interface

The HAT talks to the Pi over the hardware UART on the 40-pin header — nothing to
wire.

| Signal | Pin        | Notes                              |
|--------+------------+------------------------------------|
| TX/RX  | UART0      | NMEA sentences, 9600 baud default  |
| PPS    | GPIO4      | One pulse-per-second timing output |
| ANT    | u.FL       | Optional external active antenna   |

The HAT takes over the Pi's hardware UART, so the serial console must be freed
first (it can't share the port).

* Onboard features

- *FIX LED* — blinks while searching, ~once every 15 s once it has a fix.
- *CR1220 backup* — keeps the RTC and last almanac alive for warm starts; the
  cell is sold separately.
- *Prototyping area* — a small pad field for soldering extra parts.
- *Patch antenna* on board, with the u.FL connector for an external one.

* Mechanical

65 × 56 × 7 mm, HAT footprint.

Dual-channel 10 A DC motor driver HAT for the Raspberry Pi.

Cytron HAT-MDD10 — a dual-channel motor
driver HAT (10 A continuous per channel) that stacks on the Raspberry Pi's
40-pin header.

robot/hat_mdd10sm.py identifiers ↔ vendor labels ↔ RPi BCM
GPIOs:

Vendor uses PWM1/PWM2/DIR1/DIR2; we use AN1/AN2/DIG1/DIG2. When grepping the
datasheet, expect PWM/DIR.

VM/GND feed both channels. Logic 3.3 V comes from the Pi over the 40-pin header
— no separate logic supply needed.

Sign-magnitude (ours). Two distinct signals per channel: square-wave PWM on
ANx for speed, static high/low on DIGx for direction. Direction transitions
are clean. See HatMDD10SM.on_cmd_vel for the duty-cycle mapping from
/cmd_vel.

Locked-antiphase. ANx tied permanently high (driver enable), DIGx driven
with PWM. 50 % duty → stop; < 50 % → one direction; > 50 % → other. Useful when
PWM peripherals are scarce. We don't use this mode.

The test buttons let you confirm wiring + supply + bridge work without involving
the Pi — useful for first bring-up.
Absolute maximums — exceed and you damage the board.
No more than 10 seconds; vendor spec at 25 °C ambient.
Output frequency matches input frequency one-to-one.

67.5 × 59 mm. Fusion 360 source (cytron-hat-mdd10.f3d) and a
.step export live with the board assets in the repo.

| Label | Component               | Driver                  |
|-------+-------------------------+-------------------------|
| A     | Motor terminal block    | M1A/M1B/VM/GND/M2A/M2B  |
| B     | Motor 1 LED (A side)    |                         |
| C     | Motor 2 LED (A side)    |                         |
| D     | Motor 1 test switch     |                         |

| G     | Power LED               |                         |
| H     | PWM1 input              | ~AN1~ → ~GPIO12~         |
| I     | DIR1 input              | ~DIG1~ → ~GPIO26~        |
| J     | PWM2 input              | ~AN2~ → ~GPIO13~         |
| K     | DIR2 input              | ~DIG2~ → ~GPIO24~        |

* Driver mapping

=robot/hat_mdd10sm.py= identifiers ↔ vendor labels ↔ RPi BCM
GPIOs:

| Code   | Board    | RPi BCM  | Function            |
|--------+----------+----------+---------------------|
| ~AN1~  | H / PWM1 | ~GPIO12~ | Motor 1 speed (PWM) |
| ~DIG1~ | I / DIR1 | ~GPIO26~ | Motor 1 direction   |
| ~AN2~  | J / PWM2 | ~GPIO13~ | Motor 2 speed (PWM) |
| ~DIG2~ | K / DIR2 | ~GPIO24~ | Motor 2 direction   |

Vendor uses =PWM1/PWM2/DIR1/DIR2=; we use =AN1/AN2/DIG1/DIG2=. When grepping the
datasheet, expect =PWM/DIR=.

* Terminal block (label A)

| Pin | Function                        |
|-----+---------------------------------|
| M1A | Motor 1 — terminal A            |
| M1B | Motor 1 — terminal B            |
| VM  | Motor supply (6–24 V, max 30 A) |
| GND | Common ground                   |
| M2A | Motor 2 — terminal A            |
| M2B | Motor 2 — terminal B            |

VM/GND feed both channels. Logic 3.3 V comes from the Pi over the 40-pin header
— *no separate logic supply needed*.

* Truth table

| PWM  | DIR        | Output A | Output B | Effect                  |
|------+------------+----------+----------+-------------------------|
| Low  | don't care | Low      | Low      | Coast (motor off)       |
| High | Low        | High     | Low      | Drive A → B (one way)   |
| High | High       | Low      | High     | Drive B → A (other way) |

* PWM modes

/Sign-magnitude (ours)./ Two distinct signals per channel: square-wave PWM on
~ANx~ for speed, static high/low on ~DIGx~ for direction. Direction transitions
are clean. See ~HatMDD10SM.on_cmd_vel~ for the duty-cycle mapping from
~/cmd_vel~.

/Locked-antiphase./ ~ANx~ tied permanently high (driver enable), ~DIGx~ driven
with PWM. 50 % duty → stop; < 50 % → one direction; > 50 % → other. Useful when
PWM peripherals are scarce. *We don't use this mode.*

* Indicators & test buttons

| Label | Component   | Behavior                                                     |
|-------+-------------+--------------------------------------------------------------|
| B, C  | LED A-side  | Lit when output A high, B low — current A → B                |
| B, C  | LED B-side  | Lit when output B high, A low — current B → A                |
| G     | Power LED   | On whenever VM is present                                    |
| D, E  | Test button | Drives the H-bridge directly while pressed — bypasses the Pi |

The test buttons let you confirm wiring + supply + bridge work without involving
the Pi — useful for first bring-up.

* Electrical limits

Absolute maximums — exceed and you damage the board.

| #  | Parameter                            | Min | Typ | Max | Unit |
|----+--------------------------------------+-----+-----+-----+------|
|  1 | Motor supply voltage (~VM~)          |   6 |  –  |  24 | V    |
|  2 | Continuous motor current per channel |  –  |  –  |  10 | A    |
|  3 | Peak motor current[fn:1]             |  –  |  –  |  30 | A    |
|  4 | Logic input — high level             | 3.0 |  –  | 5.5 | V    |
|  5 | Logic input — low level              | 0.0 | 0   | 0.5 | V    |
|  6 | PWM frequency[fn:2]                  |  –  |  –  |  20 | kHz  |

[fn:1] No more than 10 seconds; vendor spec at 25 °C ambient.

[fn:2] Output frequency matches input frequency one-to-one.

* Mechanical

=.step= export live with the board assets in the repo.

single-channel bidirectional driver for one brushed DC motor, 20 A continuous
(60 A peak). Discrete NMOS H-bridge, no heatsink needed.
Three pins on the PWM/DIR header drive the one motor:

Logic inputs accept a wide 1.5–15 V, so a Raspberry Pi or Arduino GPIO drives it
directly.
Motor direction also depends on how MA~/~MB are wired — swap them to reverse.

Limited by the overcurrent circuit; the value shown is at 25–30 °C. The
limit drops as the board heats up.
Running in the extended range reduces the continuous current rating.

Overcurrent — active current limiting chops the PWM to hold current at the
  limit, so a stall or oversized motor won't destroy the board.
Temperature — the current-limit threshold falls as the board heats up.

Undervoltage — the output shuts down when the supply sags too low to drive
  the MOSFETs fully.

There is no reverse-polarity protection — wiring VB+~/~VB− backwards damages
the driver instantly.

#+title: Cytron MD20A
#+description: Single-channel 20 A DC motor driver.
#+icon: CircuitBoard

[[https://www.cytron.io/p-20amp-6v-30v-dc-motor-driver][Cytron MD20A]] — a
single-channel bidirectional driver for one brushed DC motor, 20 A continuous
(60 A peak). Discrete NMOS H-bridge, no heatsink needed.

* Board layout

[[/cytron-md20a/board-layout.webp]]

| Component             | Detail                                        |
|-----------------------+-----------------------------------------------|
| Power input terminal  | ~VB+~ / ~VB−~                                 |
| Motor output terminal | ~MA~ / ~MB~                                    |
| PWM/DIR input         | ~DIR~ / ~PWM~ / ~GND~                          |
| Power LED             | On when powered                               |
| Motor status LEDs     | ~MA~ forward, ~MB~ backward                    |
| Overcurrent LED       | On while current limiting is active           |
| Error LED             | On during undervoltage shutdown or fault      |
| Test buttons          | ~MA~ forward / ~MB~ backward, at full speed    |

* Control interface

Three pins on the ~PWM/DIR~ header drive the one motor:

| Pin | Function                          |
|-----+-----------------------------------|
| DIR | Direction — static high / low     |
| PWM | Speed — square wave, up to 20 kHz |
| GND | Shared ground with the controller |

Logic inputs accept a wide 1.5–15 V, so a Raspberry Pi or Arduino GPIO drives it
directly.

* Truth table

Motor direction also depends on how ~MA~/~MB~ are wired — swap them to reverse.

| PWM  | DIR        | Output MA | Output MB | Motor    |
|------+------------+-----------+-----------+----------|
| Low  | don't care | Low       | Low       | Brake    |
| High | Low        | High      | Low       | Forward  |
| High | High       | Low       | High      | Backward |

* Wiring

[[/cytron-md20a/wiring-diagram.webp]]

* Electrical limits

Absolute maximums — exceed and you damage the board.

| # | Parameter                     | Min | Max | Unit |
|---+-------------------------------+-----+-----+------|
| 1 | Power input voltage           |   6 |  30 | V    |
| 2 | Continuous motor current      |   – |  20 | A    |
| 3 | Peak motor current[fn:1]      |   – |  60 | A    |
| 4 | Logic input — low level       |   0 | 0.8 | V    |
| 5 | Logic input — high level      | 1.5 |  15 | V    |
| 6 | PWM frequency — standard      |  DC |  20 | kHz  |
| 7 | PWM frequency — extended[fn:2] |  20 |  40 | kHz  |

[fn:1] Limited by the overcurrent circuit; the value shown is at 25–30 °C. The
limit drops as the board heats up.

[fn:2] Running in the extended range reduces the continuous current rating.

* Protection

- *Overcurrent* — active current limiting chops the PWM to hold current at the
  limit, so a stall or oversized motor won't destroy the board.
- *Temperature* — the current-limit threshold falls as the board heats up.
- *Undervoltage* — the output shuts down when the supply sags too low to drive
  the MOSFETs fully.

There is *no reverse-polarity protection* — wiring ~VB+~/~VB−~ backwards damages
the driver instantly.

* Mechanical

86 × 52 mm, with 81 × 47 mm between the four ⌀3 mm mounting holes.

[[/cytron-md20a/dimensions.webp]]

Cytron MD30C — a
single-channel bidirectional driver for one brushed DC motor, 30 A continuous
(80 A peak). Full NMOS H-bridge, so no heatsink or fan. This is Revision 2.0.
Two logic inputs on the INPUT header drive the one motor:

Logic inputs accept 3.3 V or 5 V, so a Raspberry Pi or Arduino GPIO drives it
directly. This is not an RC (radio-control) PWM signal.

The JP4~/~JP6 jumpers pick where the speed signal comes from. We feed an
external PWM signal from the controller (bottom row):

Sign-magnitude. PWM carries speed, DIR carries direction. Direction
transitions are clean. This is how we drive it.

Locked-antiphase. DIR is fed a PWM signal: 50 % duty is stop, either side of
50 % picks a direction and speed. Frees up a PWM channel when they're scarce.

Reverse-polarity protection guards the power input. For currents above 20 A,
solder the wires directly to the bottom-layer pads rather than using the screw
terminals.
78.74 × 93.98 mm overall, with 71.12 × 86.36 mm between mounting holes.

(80 A peak). Full NMOS H-bridge, so no heatsink or fan. This is Revision 2.0.

* Board layout

[[/cytron-md30c/board-layout.webp]]

| #  | Component                                             |
|----+-------------------------------------------------------|
|  1 | Power terminal block                                  |
|  2 | Input header — ~GND~ / ~PWM~ / ~DIR~                  |
|  3 | PWM source selector (~JP4~ / ~JP6~)                   |
|  4 | Internal PWM potentiometer                            |
|  5 | External PWM potentiometer port (10 kΩ)               |
|  6 | Test button A — output A → B                          |
|  7 | Test button B — output B → A                          |
|  8 | Motor terminal block                                  |
|  9 | Red LED A — lit when output A high, B low             |
| 10 | Red LED B — lit when output B high, A low             |
| 11 | Green power LED                                        |

* Control interface

Two logic inputs on the ~INPUT~ header drive the one motor:

| Pin | Function                          |
|-----+-----------------------------------|
| GND | Shared ground with the controller |
| PWM | Speed — square wave, up to 20 kHz |
| DIR | Direction — static high / low     |

Logic inputs accept 3.3 V or 5 V, so a Raspberry Pi or Arduino GPIO drives it
directly. This is *not* an RC (radio-control) PWM signal.

* PWM source

The ~JP4~/~JP6~ jumpers pick where the speed signal comes from. We feed an
external PWM signal from the controller (bottom row):

| Source                 | ~JP4~   | ~JP6~   |
|------------------------+---------+---------|
| Internal potentiometer | INT POT | INT PWM |
| External potentiometer | EXT POT | INT PWM |
| External PWM signal    | X       | EXT PWM |

| PWM  | DIR        | Motor              |
|------+------------+--------------------|
| Low  | don't care | Stop (coast)       |
| High | Low        | Turn one way       |
| High | High       | Turn the other way |

* PWM modes

/Sign-magnitude./ ~PWM~ carries speed, ~DIR~ carries direction. Direction
transitions are clean. This is how we drive it.

/Locked-antiphase./ ~DIR~ is fed a PWM signal: 50 % duty is stop, either side of
50 % picks a direction and speed. Frees up a PWM channel when they're scarce.

Absolute maximums — exceed and you damage the board.

| # | Parameter                    | Min | Typ | Max | Unit |
|---+------------------------------+-----+-----+-----+------|

| 2 | Continuous motor current     |   – |   – |  30 | A    |
| 3 | Peak motor current[fn:1]     |   – |   – |  80 | A    |
| 4 | Idle current                 |   – |   – | 100 | mA   |
| 5 | Logic input — high level     |   3 |   – | 5.5 | V    |
| 6 | Logic input — low level      |   0 |   0 | 0.5 | V    |
| 7 | PWM frequency[fn:2]          |   – |   – |  20 | kHz  |

[fn:1] Must not exceed 1 second.

[fn:2] Output frequency matches input frequency one-to-one.

Reverse-polarity protection guards the power input. For currents above 20 A,

#+title: User Manual
#+description: Setup, operation, and safety for the rover.
#+icon: BookOpen

The *rover* is a rugged, semi-autonomous mobile robot
built for agricultural field work. This manual covers ~unboxing~, first power-on,
day-to-day /operation/, and safety. For tutorials and API reference, see the
[[https://www.tandemrobotics.ca][documentation home]].

#+begin_quote
Read *Safety Considerations* before operating the rover for the first time.
#+end_quote

* Introduction

** Shipment Contents

Every rover ships with the following:

- Rover chassis
  - Four-wheel drivetrain with independent suspension
  - Sealed battery bay
- Battery pack and charger
- Wireless stop remote
- Optional add-ons
  - Payload mounting kit
  - Futaba RC controller

** Hardware Overview

*** System Architecture

The rover runs a two-tier compute stack:

- Onboard computer :: Runs ROS 2 and the autonomy stack (planning, perception, localization).
- Microcontroller :: Handles real-time motor control and hardware safety cutoffs.

Motor control runs through the
[[id:9a3c1e70-8b21-4d55-9e10-1f2a3b4c5d02][Cytron HAT-MDD10]] driver board.

*** Body Lights

Body-light color maps directly to rover state:

| Color | State                   |
|-------+-------------------------|
| Green | Ready / autonomous      |
| Blue  | Manual / teleop         |
| Red   | Emergency-stopped       |
| Amber | Fault / needs attention |

| Dimensions | TODO  |

* Getting Started

** Powering Up

1. Insert the battery and latch the retention clip.
2. Turn the main key switch to ~ON~.
3. Wait for the body lights to turn *green* before commanding motion.

On a healthy boot you should see:

#+begin_example
[  ok  ] tandem-bringup.service
[  ok  ] ros2-daemon.service
rover ready — state: IDLE
#+end_example

** Using ROS

Bring up the driver and list the active topics:

#+begin_src bash
ros2 launch tandem_bringup rover.launch.py
ros2 topic list
#+end_src

Drive the rover by publishing a velocity command to =/cmd_vel=:

#+begin_src bash
ros2 topic pub /cmd_vel geometry_msgs/msg/Twist "{linear: {x: 0.5}}"
#+end_src

The legacy +/tandem/cmd+ topic has been replaced by =/cmd_vel=.

** Network Configuration

Set the field network in the rover config, then restart the bringup service:

#+begin_src yaml
wifi:
  ssid: tandem-field
  password: changeme
#+end_src

* Safety Considerations

#+begin_quote
*Warning:* In autonomous mode the rover can begin moving without further input.
Keep the wireless stop remote within reach at all times.
#+end_quote

** Pinch Points

Keep hands clear of the suspension travel and wheel wells while the rover is
powered, even when idle.

** Stop Buttons

Press any physical stop button, or the wireless remote, to cut motor power
immediately.[fn:estop]

-----

[fn:estop] Every stop path is hardware-level and independent of the software
stack, so it works even if the onboard computer has hung.
